             Manikyamma, Anasuyamma, Madhusudhan Reddy and Janardhan

             Reddy entered into a family settlement on 19.04.1959, delineating their
separate shares in the ancestral properties left behind by B.Venkat Reddy.

In terms thereof, Manikyamma was given Acres(Ac.) 53-10 Guntas (Gts.)

of land in Karkalpahad Village. Anasuyamma was given Ac. 40-01 Gts. in

Karkalpahad Village; Ac. 28-38 Gts. in Kadthal Village; Ac. 14-12 Gts. in

Vasudevapuram Village and Ac. 8-11 Gts. in Vampuguda Village. In all,

she was given Ac. 91-22 Gts. Madhusudhan Reddy was allotted Ac. 1-30

Gts. in Karkalpahad Village and Ac. 60-19 Gts. in Vasudevapuram Village.

In all, he got Ac. 62-09 Gts. Janardhan Reddy was given Ac. 50-10 Gts.

in Karkalpahad Village along with Ac. 56-14 Gts. in Vampuguda Village

and Ac. 24-23 Gts. in Kadthal Village. In all, he got Ac. 131-07 Gts.

4.    While so, Anasuyamma and her adopted son, Venkatraji Reddy,

filed O.S. No. 555 of 1977 before the learned I Additional Judge, City Civil

Court, Hyderabad, seeking partition of the suit schedules A, B and C

properties. Manikyamma was arrayed as defendant No. 1 in the said suit

while Madhusudhan Reddy and Janardhan Reddy, her sons, were shown

as defendant Nos. 2 and 3 respectively. As Madhusudhan Reddy had sold

certain properties, the vendees independently filed O.S. No. 21 of 1977

before the learned Subordinate Judge, Mahabubnagar, for declaration of

title along with a permanent injunction to protect their rights. This suit was

transferred to the file of the learned I Additional Judge, City Civil Court,

Hyderabad, to be tried along with O.S. No. 555 of 1977 and was

renumbered as O.S. No. 263 of 1978. By common judgment dated
                                      2
21.04.1984, the Trial Court decreed O.S. No. 263 of 1978 and partly

decreed O.S. No. 555 of 1977, directing partition of the suit schedules B

and C properties. Insofar as the suit schedule A properties were

concerned, the Trial Court held that the same were covered by the family

settlement dated 19.04.1959 and dismissed the suit in relation thereto.

5.    Aggrieved by the judgment dated 21.04.1984 insofar as it pertained

to part decretal of O.S. No. 555 of 1977, Madhusudhan Reddy filed City

Civil Court Appeal (CCCA) No. 86 of 1984 before the then Andhra Pradesh

High Court at Hyderabad. During the pendency of O.S. No. 555 of 1977,

Janardhan Reddy had died and his son, Venkat Reddy, was brought on

record as his legal representative. His sister, Nirmala, who was not a party

to O.S. No. 555 of 1977, filed CCCA No. 54 of 1989 assailing the judgment

dated 21.04.1984 insofar as it pertained to the said suit.

6.    While the aforestated appeals were pending before the High Court,

a compromise was arrived at by and between Anasuyamma along with

her adopted son, Venkatraji Reddy, and Madhusudhan Reddy, the

appellant in CCCA No. 86 of 1984. The terms of the said compromise

were reduced to writing in the document titled ‘Settlement of Dispute’

dated 24.02.1986. Pursuant thereto, Civil Miscellaneous Petition (CMP)

No. 9728 of 1988 was filed by Madhusudhan Reddy under Order XXIII,

Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, to record the settlement dated

24.02.1986 and decree the appeal in terms thereof. This miscellaneous
                                     3
petition was ordered on 27.06.1988 and the compromise, reflected in the

Settlement of Dispute Deed dated 24.02.1986, was recorded.

7.    In terms of the said settlement, Anasuyamma and her adopted son,

Venkatraji Reddy, gave up their claim for a 1/3rd share in the suit schedule

B house property at Door No. 3-6-375, Himayatnagar, Hyderabad, and

Madhusudhan Reddy was given the said house property absolutely.

Madhusudhan Reddy, in turn, gave up his claim for a share in the

properties of his mother, Manikyamma, and the same were surrendered

to Anasuyamma and Venkatraji Reddy. Anasuyamma and Venkatraji

Reddy also gave up their claim for a 1/3rd share in the suit schedule C

house property situated at Karkalpahad Village. A sum of ₹2,20,000/- was

paid by Madhusudhan Reddy to Anasuyamma and Venkatraji Reddy.

8.    By judgment dated 07.09.1990, the High Court allowed CCCA No.

86 of 1984, in the light of the compromise by Madhusudhan Reddy with

Anasuyamma and Venkatraji Reddy and also the settlement between

Madhusudhan Reddy and Venkat Reddy, the son of Janardhan Reddy.

However, as regards CCCA No. 54 of 1986 filed by Nirmala, the sister of

Venkat Reddy, the High Court dismissed the said appeal leaving it open

to her to work out her rights by way of a separate suit.

9.    While matters stood thus, Madhusudhan Reddy executed registered

Gift Deed No. 4257 of 2007 dated 24.04.2007 in favour of Siddhartha

Reddy, the son of Venkat Reddy, that is, the grandson of Janardhan
                                     4
Reddy, gifting him various lands. This Gift Deed pertained to lands in

Survey Nos. 2, 70, 130, 135, 136 and 137 of Karkalpahad Village.

Significantly, allotment of lands to Madhusudhan Reddy under the family

settlement dated 19.04.1959 reflects that the lands gifted by him did not

fall to his share. He was only given Ac. 1-30 Gts. in Survey No. 15 of

Karkalpahad Village and had, therefore, no claim in the lands that found

mention in the gift geed. In fact, the lands that found mention therein were

allotted to Manikyamma and Madhusudan Reddy had given up his claim

in those lands when he compromised his disputes with Anasuyamma and

her adopted son, Venkatraji Reddy, vide the Settlement of Dispute Deed

dated 24.02.1986, which had the imprimatur of the High Court, vide the

judgment dated 07.09.1990 in CCCA No. 86 of 1984.

10.   Anasuyamma and her adopted son, Venkatraji Reddy, along with his

by-birth sister, Gunna Malinidevi, thereupon, filed O.S. No. 250 of 2007

before the learned Senior Civil Judge, Mahabubnagar, for declaration of

their title over the suit schedule lands; to declare Gift Deed No. 4257 of

2007 dated 24.04.2007 as null and void; to effect necessary mutation in

the revenue records; and to permanently injunct the defendants from

interfering with their possession over the suit schedule lands. The suit

schedule lands were Ac. 3-17 Gts. in Survey No. 121/AA, Ac. 0-33 Gts. in

Survey No. 130/A, Ac. 5-33 Gts. in Survey No. 131/2, Ac. 3-34 Gts. in

Survey No. 135/A, Ac. 1-11 Gts. in Survey No. 136/AA, Ac. 0-38 Gts. in
                                     5
Survey No. 137/A and Ac. 2-12 Gts. in Survey No. 2 of Karkalpahad

Village. Pertinent to note, Gunna Malinidevi had purchased an extent of

Ac. 1-22 Gts. in Survey No. 2 of Karkalpahad Village from Venkatraji

Reddy under registered sale deed dated 15.05.1998. The defendants in

the suit were Madhusudhan Reddy, Venkat Reddy and his son,

Siddhartha Reddy. Anasuyamma died during the pendency of the suit.

11.   By judgment dated 09.04.2012, the learned Senior Civil Judge,

Mahabubnagar, dismissed the suit. Surprisingly, the learned Judge opined

therein that the compromise decree dated 07.09.1990 in CCCA No. 86 of

1984 had no evidentiary value. Holding so, the learned Judge completely

ignored the compromise by Madhusudhan Reddy with Anasuyamma and

Venkatraji Reddy and proceeded to hold against them.

12.   Aggrieved by the dismissal of their suit, Venkatraji Reddy and

Gunna Malinidevi filed Appeal Suit No. 372 of 2012 before the Telangana

High Court at Hyderabad, which was dismissed by judgment dated

12.12.2022. Surprisingly, the learned Judge of the High Court, having set

out at great length the chronology of events and the arguments advanced

by the learned counsel, failed to draw the correct inferences from the past

history, in terms of the family settlement of 1959 and the compromise of

1986, which had the seal of approval of the High Court, vide the judgment

dated 07.09.1990 in CCCA No. 86 of 1994. Non-application of mind by the

learned Judge is patent from the observation that ‘execution of the Gift
                                    6
Deed dated 24.04.2007 was never disputed’. In saying so, the learned

Judge lost sight of the fact that O.S. No. 250 of 2007 was filed on

21.08.2007 challenging the said gift deed. Compounding her error, the

learned Judge then observed that Manikyamma died during the pendency

of the suit and was not entitled to any share and, therefore, the claim of

Venkatraji Reddy that he was in enjoyment of the property allotted to her

had no merit. This finding was based on the failure of the learned Judge

to note the contents of the family settlement dated 19.04.1959, which was

accepted by Madhusudan Reddy also, and the compromise dated

24.02.1986, whereby Madhusudhan Reddy gave up his claim for a share

in the properties allotted to Manikyamma in the family settlement of 1959

and secured full rights in the house property at Himayatnagar, Hyderabad.

13.   Founded on such fundamental errors, the judgments of the High

Court and the Trial Court cannot be sustained. Notably, despite service of

notice, none of the respondents in this appeal chose to appear.

Madhusudhan Reddy and Venkat Reddy are Respondent Nos. 1 and 2,

but as they had expired even during the pendency of the appeal before

the High Court, they are shown as represented by their legal heirs.

Siddhartha Reddy, son of Venkat Reddy, is respondent No. 3, while

Hemalatha, Madhusudhan Reddy’s widow, is respondent No. 4. Vijayata

Devi, the widow of Venkat Reddy, and Rukmini and Sirisha, his daughters,

are respondent Nos. 6 to 8. Third parties to whom Siddhartha Reddy
                                    7
sought to alienate some lands were respondent Nos. 5, 6 and 7 before

the High Court and they are respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 in this appeal.

However, as stated earlier, none of the respondents chose to enter

appearance before this Court to contest this appeal. Significantly, by order

dated 16.05.2023, this Court had directed status quo obtaining as on that

date, with regard to the nature and possession over the lands in dispute,

to be maintained. Despite such an order being passed against them, none

of the respondents chose to come forward to contest the appeal. Their

failure to do so speaks for itself.

14.   The appeal is, accordingly, allowed setting aside the judgment and

decree dated 12.12.2022 in AS No. 372 of 2012 and the judgment and

decree dated 09.04.2012 in O.S. No. 250 of 2007. The said suit shall stand

decreed, as prayed for.

      There shall be no orders as to costs.

5.   The Madhya Pradesh Sand (Mining, Transportation, Storage

     materially amended on 26.05.2023. Under the arrangement

     quarry leases, while the MDO selected for a particular group

     statutory permissions governing the individual mines.

       State action in the award of public contracts. The law in this

     invalidation of arrest as the consequence of delayed
     forwarding.
7.   Mere similarity between grounds of arrest and reasons to
     believe does not cause prejudice to the Appellant. The relevant
     test, in this regards, is whether the accused was made aware of
     the essential basis of his arrest and whether the Special Court
     was able to examine the existence of material and recorded
     satisfaction u/S. 19(1). That the core safeguards against

SLP (Crl.) No. 10994 of 2026                            Page 5 of 9
     arbitrary arrest were duly complied with: the authorised officer
     had material in possession, reasons to believe were recorded in
     writing, grounds of arrest were furnished and the Appellant
     was produced before the competent court within 24 hours. That
     grave economic offence involving proceeds of Crime is more
     than Rs. 6,210.72 Crores. That the Appellant is involved in
     over 444 cases.
8.   Heard. Records perused.
9.   In a bail matter, especially in serious offences, the job of a
     Court is to balance the rights of the State with those of the
     Arrestee. In special laws such as PMLA, 2002, the conditions
     for granting bail are stringent, and the circumstances in which
     bail can be granted are rare, for the simple reason that
     economic offences of a large magnitude punch a whole through
     the financial fabric of the country, causing a top-down ripple
     effect into the entire eco-system resulting in large
     consequences for most of the population. That is the
     justification for making the provisions of PMLA stringent. In
     the same breath, sight must not be lost of the fact that the
     institutions have a duty to expeditiously investigate the cases,
     or else the justification to keep an accused person under




SLP (Crl.) No. 10994 of 2026                             Page 6 of 9
    custody for an indefinite period of time. Process must not be
    turned into a punishment unto itself.
10. We do not agree with the contention of the Ld. Counsel for the
    Appellant that the arrest was rendered illegal and there was
    non-compliance of Section 19(2) because there was a delay of
    5 days in forwarding the arrest order and material in possession
    to the Adjudicating Authority. The reason is simple. There is
    no timeline mentioned in PMLA to forward the arrest order and
    the material in possession to the Adjudicating Authority. It has
    to be done “immediately”. The word “immediately” does not
    mean within 24 hours or within a set time limit, it means that
    the material has to be transferred expeditiously and
    simultaneously. When the records of the case run into
    thousands of pages, it is natural for the arresting officer to
    require some time to forward the same. Again, this time cannot
    be strictly defined, but as long as the forwarding of the material
    is simultaneous with the arrest, with no delay, except for that
    which is absolutely necessary, the same cannot be said to be
    falling foul of Section 19(2) of the Act. Practicalities must not
    be rendered otiose. When an investigating agency is collecting,
    assimilating, and compiling evidence to be forwarded, there
    can be administrative requirements which need to be fulfilled

3.    The Corporate Debtor/M/s Samyu Glass Private Limited, a Company

1963”) is synonymous with the statutory “period of limitation” computed in

accordance with the Act. Any discretionary window beyond the prescribed

period, i.e., during which an Appellate Tribunal or court may condone delay

on sufficient cause, cannot be treated as part of the prescribed period.

8.    In V. Nagarajan (supra), this Court considered the scheme of the IBC

and, in parallel, examined the applicability of the provisions of the Act, 1963

to the IBC. Instead of culling out the excerpts, we will paraphrase the ratio of

V. Nagarajan (supra) as follows:

A.    The IBC is an exhaustive, self-contained code. By virtue of the non-

obstante clause in Section 238 of the IBC, its provisions prevail over any

inconsistencies with other statutes. While Section 238-A of the IBC applies

the provisions of the Act, 1963 “as far as may be”, this is subject to Section

29(2) of the Act, 1963. Where a special statute provides a distinct period of

limitation, that period governs to the exclusion of general provisions, and the

IBC, being a special law, would have an overriding effect. Section 61(1) of the

IBC starts with a non-obstante clause. Consequently, the appellate

mechanisms under the Companies Act cannot control or relax the statutory

architecture of the IBC.

B.    Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 mandates that every Appeal be

accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned Order. Section 12(2) of the

Act, 1963 excludes the time required to obtain a copy of the impugned Order.

The Explanation to Section 12 of the Act, 1963 makes it clear that any time

the Tribunal or Court takes to prepare the Order before the litigant applies for

a copy cannot be excluded. If a party fails to apply for a certified copy within


                                       6
the limitation period, no time can be excluded under Section 12(2) of the Act,

1963. Applying for a certified copy is not a mere procedural formality; it

reflects the aggrieved party's due diligence.

C.    Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a 30-day period for filing an Appeal,

extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause,

and no more. Courts and Tribunals have no power under Section 5 of the Act,

1963, or inherent powers to condone delays beyond the outer limit of 15 days

prescribed in special statutes. The IBC's foundational architecture weaves

speed and strict timelines to preserve asset value, maximise recovery for

lenders, and protect economic health. Procedural rules cannot be interpreted

to protract litigation indefinitely.

9.    Similarly, and closer to the case at hand, is CA Ramchandra Dallaram

Choudhary (supra). The gist of the findings is as follows:


A.    The IBC’s limitation scheme is strict and time-bound, making

condonation of delay outside the statutory framework impermissible. Under

Section 62 of the IBC, the absolute outer limit for filing an appeal is 60 days,

i.e., the standard 45-day period plus a 15-day grace period upon showing

sufficient cause. Beyond this period, the Court loses jurisdiction to condone

any delay.

B.    The right to appeal is permanently extinguished once the 60-day

maximum window under the IBC closes and the 28-day window under the

Supreme Court Rules, 2013 (“SCR, 2013”) for curing defects lapses.

C.    The SCR, 2013 are subordinate legislation and cannot override the

IBC’s express provisions. Therefore, the SCR, 2013 cannot grant an extended

                                       7
window for re-filing if doing so would contravene the legislative intent behind

the IBC's strict timelines.

10.   Under Section 238-A of the IBC, the Act, 1963 applies to proceedings

and appeals under the Code “as far as may be.” The relevant statutory

provisions are set out below:


              “Section 238-A, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,
              2016:
              238-A. Limitation.—The provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963
              (36 of 1963) shall, as far as may be, apply to the
              proceedings or appeals before the Adjudicating Authority, the
              National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, the Debt
              Recovery Tribunal or the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal,
              as the case may be.”

                                     xxx.            xxx
              “Section 12, Limitation Act, 1963:
              "12. Exclusion of time in legal proceedings.— (1)
                                      xxx           xxx
              (2) In computing the period of limitation for an appeal or an
              application for leave to appeal or for revision or for review of
              a judgment, the day on which the judgment complained of
              was pronounced and the time requisite for obtaining a copy
              of the decree, sentence or order appealed from or sought to
              be revised or reviewed shall be excluded.
                                     xxx             xxx
              Explanation.—In computing under this section the time
              requisite for obtaining a copy of a decree or an order, any time
              taken by the court to prepare the decree or order before an
              application for a copy thereof is made shall not be excluded.”

                                                    (emphasis supplied)

11.   A clear distinction exists between the exclusion of time under Section

12 of the Limitation Act and the condonation of delay under Section 62(2) of

the IBC. Section 62 provides an initial limitation period of 45 days from the

date of receipt of the order, extendable by a discretionary condonable period

of up to 15 days, creating an absolute outer ceiling of 60 days.

12.   The phrase “from the date of receipt of the order” in Section 62(1) cannot

be read as the date on which a party chooses to apply for and collect a certified

copy. If the limitation clock remained suspended until physical collection at
                                             8
the litigant’s leisure, the limitation period would then become fluctuating and

indefinite. Furthermore, Section 12(2) of the Act, 1963 would be rendered

wholly redundant. There would be no reason for Parliament to make the

exclusion of "time requisite for obtaining a copy" applicable via Section 238-A

of the IBC if limitation did not already commence upon pronouncement.

13.   The above precedents reinforce this distinction. In Sagufa Ahmed

(supra), this Court held that limitation under Section 421(3) of the Companies

Act, 2013, ran from the receipt of the judgment, because Section 420(3), read

with Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, created a statutory right to receive a

free certified copy. Conversely, as held in V. Nagarajan (supra), the IBC is a

complete Code that overrides the Companies Act, 2013 under Section 238 of

the IBC. For an appeal to the Supreme Court under Section 62 of the IBC, the

requirements and procedure for obtaining and filing a certified copy are

governed by Order XIX Rule 3(2)(i), read with Rule 40 of the SCR, 2013.

Because these provisions impose an affirmative obligation on the Appellant to

proactively apply for and produce a certified copy, a litigant cannot claim to

await a copy to keep the limitation period suspended.

14.   Further, Rule 91 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 reads as follows:


             “91. Pronouncement of order.-
             (1) The Appellate Tribunal shall as far as possible pronounce
             the order immediately after the hearing is concluded.
             (2) When the orders are reserved, the date for pronouncement
             of order shall be notified in the cause list which shall be a
             valid notice of intimation of pronouncement.
             (3) Reading of the operative portion of the order in the
             open court shall be deemed to be pronouncement of the
             order.”
                                                 (emphasis supplied)




                                           9
       On a bare reading of the Rule mandating pronouncement of the Order

in open Court, knowledge and limitation would commence on the day the Rule

is complied with. Consequently, the limitation period commences on the date

the NCLAT pronounces the Order for an Appeal to this Court under Section

62 of the IBC. Under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, only the “time

requisite” for obtaining a copy, i.e., the period between the filing of the

Application and the date the certified copy is ready, is excluded. Under the

Explanation to Section 12 of the Act, 1963, any period of inaction before filing

the Application for a certified copy cannot be excluded and must be deducted

from the statutory limitation period.


15.    The following circumstances are noted:


  i.   The NCLAT pronounced the impugned Judgment on 02.08.2023.

 ii.   The Appellant applied for a certified copy on 06.09.2023 (the 35th day).

       The 35 days of inaction before filing the Application cannot be excluded

       and count directly against the initial 45-day statutory window.

iii.   The Application remained pending with the Registry from 06.09.2023

       until delivery on 11.10.2023 (35 days). This period constitutes “time

       requisite” under Section 12(2) of the Act, 1963, and is therefore

       excluded.

iv.    Upon receipt of the certified copy on 11.10.2023, the limitation clock

       resumed. Having already consumed 35 days of the initial 45-day

       window, the Appellant had 10 days remaining to file within the

       statutory period (expiring on 21.10.2023) and a further 15 discretionary

       days under Section 62(2) (expiring on 05.11.2023).
                                        10
 v.   The Appellant did not file the Appeal until 21.11.2023, consuming

      another 41 days after receipt of the copy.


16.   Summing the actionable periods, i.e., 35 days before applying for the

certified copy and 41 days after receiving it, yields a total of 76 days. The

absolute statutory ceiling under Section 62 of the IBC is 60 days, i.e., 45 days

plus 15 condonable days. Even after excluding the time taken to prepare the

certified copy, the Appeal was filed 16 days beyond the absolute outer limit of

this Court's jurisdiction to condone delay. Applying the above discussion to

the present case, the Appeal is beyond the limitation period.

17.   If the Appellant's argument that the limitation period begins on the day

the copy of the Order is received is accepted, it would nullify both the

limitation period and the condonable period, and make the right of Appeal

subject to an indefinite and fluctuating period of limitation.

18.   The preliminary objection is accordingly sustained. The Civil Appeal

stands dismissed as barred by limitation. No order as to costs.

19.   Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

16.   Aggrieved by the judgment of the Division Bench, the Appellant-

College and other self-financing professional colleges, represented by the

Association of Professional Academic Institutes, West Bengal, are in

appeal before us.

17.   We have heard Mr. Jaideep Gupta, Mr. Harin Raval, and Mr. Rauf

Rahim, learned Senior Advocates for the Appellants, and Mr. Sanjay R.

Hegde, learned Senior Advocate for the Respondents.

Analysis

18.   The determination of fees payable for professional education

imparted through self-financing higher educational institutions involves

three legitimate interests which must coordinate and operate together.

The first is the interest of students and parents in certainty and

predictability about the reasonable fee payable for the course. The second

is the interest of self-financing educational institutions in securing

adequate resources for providing quality education and also for the future

development of the institution. The third is the societal interest,

represented by the fee fixation committees and the concerned

government, to ensure fixation of reasonable and appropriate fee, and

also the appropriate timeframe for effective and efficient implementation.


Interests of Students and Teachers

19.   An empirical study based on data collected by the National

Statistical Office (‘NSO’) examining the socio-economic and institutional




                                    14
factors determining household expenditure on professional higher

education in India6 suggested that:

               “The annual average household expenditure on higher
               education in India is Rs.26,400, which accounts for 17.3%
               of the total annual household consumption expenditure in
               2017-2018. Fees accounted for 61.2%, and non-fee
               spending constituted 38.8% of the overall spending.
               Although this is the picture for overall higher education, we
               notice a significant difference in household spending
               between general and professional courses. Students
               pursing professional courses spent remarkably higher on
               their education (483% more) than those attending general
               courses. Households spend around 46.7% and 9.7% of
               their annual consumption expenditure if one of their children
               is pursuing a professional course and general course,
               respectively, marking a huge difference. This is largely due
               to higher fees charged (particularly in private institutions) in
               professional courses such as engineering, management,
               medicine and law. Estimates reveal that the fee charged in
               professional courses is reported to be 711% more than in
               general courses.” 7


Thus, the aforesaid study reveals that students pursuing professional

courses spend remarkably higher amount on their education and the

estimates reveal that fee charged in professional courses is reported to

be 711% more than the general courses.

20.    For the overwhelming majority of households, the fee payable for a

professional course constitutes a substantial part of the family’s income

and savings; it is not a matter of incidental expenditure. The parents make

the aspiration that their children will acquire better qualifications, secure

better opportunities, and build a future that may be better than their own.

Many students and families also depend on educational loans to finance

professional higher education.

21.   It is a matter of good governance for the state and its regulatory

bodies to create an ecosystem in which there is certainty about the

financial obligation that students and their families need to undertake for

acquiring professional qualifications. Adverse variations in financial

commitment, and the insecurities that it may create, will impact the student

and the family, and, in the long run, have an adverse effect on the quality

and character of the professionals that are in the making. We are of the

opinion that it is not difficult to formulate a scheme through which such

uncertainties can be avoided.

Participation of Private Enterprise in Nation Building and the Need
to Secure Their Interests

22.   Our nation’s demand for high-quality professional education cannot

realistically be sustained exclusively through public resources. In this

backdrop, private enterprise contributes meaningfully in building our

nation’s higher educational system. The role of such private enterprise in




                                     16
higher educational institutions is recognised in TMA Pai Foundation and

Others v. State of Karnataka and Others,8 wherein this Court held

               “48. Private education is one of the most dynamic and
               fastest-growing segments of post-secondary education at
               the turn of the twenty-first century. A combination of
               unprecedented demand for access to higher education and
               the inability or unwillingness of the Government to provide
               the necessary support has brought private higher education
               to the forefront. Private institutions, with a long history in
               many countries, are expanding in scope and number, and
               are becoming increasingly important in parts of the world
               that relied almost entirely on the public sector.
               49. Not only has demand overwhelmed the ability of the
               Governments to provide education, there has also been a
               significant change in the way that higher education is
               perceived. The idea of an academic degree as a “private
               good” that benefits the individual rather than a “public good”
               for society is now widely accepted. The logic of today's
               economics and an ideology of privatization have contributed
               to the resurgence of private higher education, and the
               establishing of private institutions where none or very few
               existed before.”

23.    This Court also recognised the role of private unaided professional

colleges and held as follows:

               “70. It is well established all over the world that those who
               seek professional education must pay for it. The number of
               seats available in government and government-aided
               colleges is very small, compared to the number of persons
               seeking admission to the medical and engineering colleges.
               All those eligible and deserving candidates who could not
               be accommodated in government colleges would stand
               deprived of professional education. This void in the field of
               medical and technical education has been filled by
               institutions that are established in different places with the
               aid of donations and the active part taken by public-minded
               individuals. The object of establishing an institution has thus
               been to provide technical or professional education to the

               deserving candidates, and is not necessarily a commercial

               professional educational institution has to get recognition

24.    Self-financing         institutions       necessarily         require       substantial

investment in land, buildings, facilities, student services, libraries,

equipment, technology, and the like. They must be capable of drawing

and retaining competent teaching faculty and other professional staff by

providing them suitable, if not attractive, remuneration. After meeting

legitimate operational and developmental expenditure, the institutions

must also be permitted a reasonable return for sustenance and further

development.

The Institutional Mechanism for Balancing the Interests of Students
and Educational Institutions

25.    In pursuance of the judgment of this Court in TMA Pai Foundation

(supra) and subsequent decisions,9 a regulatory mechanism has been

evolved, as the State Legislatures have enacted laws and the State

Governments have constituted regulatory committees to establish an

objective mechanism for fixation of fees payable by the students. A

regulatory framework relevant for the purposes of the controversy

26.    It is noteworthy that NEP-2020 articulates a commitment to ensure

that there is no arbitrariness in the increase of fees in respect of

professional courses. It also contains a clear articulation of a policy

position against unjustified increases in the fee during a period of students’

enrolment.

27.    The real question is whether the institutions and regulatory

committees entrusted with this responsibility are discharging their

functions efficiently and within a timeframe that gives meaningful certainty

to students, parents, and educational institutions alike.

28.    The fee fixation committees established pursuant to this Court’s

direction in Islamic Academy and PA Inamdar are discharging an

important function. It is necessary for the High Courts to ensure that these

bodies are in a position to effectively and efficiently perform their

obligations, as their recommendations have a direct bearing on the

aspiring students’ access to higher educational opportunities and the

participating private enterprises’ interest in establishing world-class

institutions. In the context of the compelling need to institutionalize the

functioning of such bodies and the important role which High Courts

exercise in ensuring that these bodies function effectively, this Court in

Lifecare Innovations Pvt. Ltd. and Another v. Union of India and Others11

held:

              “22. While exercising judicial review of administrative action
              in the context of Statutes, laws, rules or policies establishing
              statutory or administrative bodies to implement the
              provisions of the Act or its policy, the first duty of

              23. Shifting the focus of judicial review to functional

              transcend the standard power of judicial review to issue

              effectively and efficiently. By ensuring institutional integrity
              we achieve our institutional objectives. Further, effective

           and efficient performance of the institutes can reduce

29.   Institutional efficiency is not a matter of administrative convenience.

It is an essential component of fair and effective regulation. Certainty for

the students, sustainability for the institution, and efficiency in the

regulatory process are not competing objectives; they are complementary

elements of a sound system of professional education. The question,

therefore, is not whether a fee revision can take place, but the method and

manner in which it is undertaken, concluded, and put into effect.

30.   A conjoint reading of Regulations 7(1), 7(4), and 7(5) of the AICTE

Regulations 1994 makes it clear that: (a) a revision of fees is permissible

only through the recommendation of the Committee, (b) it can be revised

only with a minimum gap of 3 years from the date of revision, (c) the

revision can only be on the recommendations based on estimated

expenditure of the professional colleges for efficient functioning, and (d)

while calculating the fees, the estimates of recurring expenditure shall be

based on at least the last two years audited figures of recurring

expenditure of the college and projected requirement of next three years.

31.   Revised fees represent the cost of education determined at the

relevant point of time. If such cost is not recovered from the students at

the relevant time and is deferred to future batches, an inevitable revenue

deficit would certainly arise and will either have a cascading effect on
                                     22
future batches or adversely affect the economic viability of the institution.

It will have its own fallout on the infrastructure, quality of lecturers and

professors, and also adversely affect student welfare. It is therefore

necessary to have periodic and effective revision of the fee payable as per

the regulations. In undertaking such revision, it is also necessary to adopt

and apply the principle of certainty with respect to the fees payable for the

professional course into which the student is admitted. This normative

principle is recognised in the AICTE Regulations 1994.

32.   Institutional efficiency compels fee fixation committees to make

recommendations well in advance and the competent authorities to take

decisions well before the commencement of the admission process. The

committee should examine the relevant costs, including infrastructure,

faculty remuneration, maintenance, technology, statutory requirements,

and other legitimate expenditure, make a reasonable assessment of

foreseeable increases in such costs over the duration of the course, and

make recommendations so that the competent authorities take the

decision before the commencement of the course. A student entering a

four-or five-year professional programme should ordinarily know, at the

very threshold, the financial liability that they or their family is undertaking.

Such advance determination promotes transparency, enables informed

choice, and facilitates financial planning. This does not mean that the fee


                                       23
structure must remain incapable of adjustment in every conceivable

circumstance. Costs may increase unexpectedly because of extraordinary

economic conditions, statutory changes or other circumstances which

could not reasonably have been anticipated. A narrowly defined

mechanism may therefore be provided to accommodate such exceptional

circumstances. But such adjustment must remain an exception and

cannot become a substitute for timely assessment and proper institutional

planning.

33.   The larger principle is thus one of certainty through efficient

regulation. The fee fixation committees must function as continuing

institutions,   capable   of   anticipating   costs,   undertaking   periodic

assessments, and making timely decisions. Its processes should be

structured so that the fee determination is completed before admissions

commence and, as far as reasonably possible, covers the entire duration

of the professional course.

34.   We may advert to the facts of the cases in hand. The fee for

professional courses in West Bengal was last revised in the 2016-17 AY.

The fee fixation committee and the State Government acted inefficiently

inasmuch as they failed to ensure the completion of revision exercise in

time for 2023-27 courses. A fresh revision of fee was undertaken after

seven years vide notification dated 16.10.2023. The Appellant-College


                                      24
adopted the revised fee on 15.12.2023. The Appellant-College cannot be

blamed for its anxiety in implementing the revised fee structure after

conclusion of the first semester. The problem arising out of mid-stream

implementation of revised fee schedule could have been avoided, if the

State Government had issued the notification dated 16.10.2023 before the

commencement of academic session 2023-2024. We can take judicial

notice of the fact that functioning of the fee fixation committees as of now

and the State’s action on their recommendations have often not been up

to the mark. The instant case demonstrates such one case.

35.   While we uphold the conclusions drawn by the Division Bench of the

High Court for the independent reasons that we have given, we are not in

agreement with the reasoning of the Division Bench that the

implementation of the revised fee structure for the 2023-27 course will

have the effect of giving retrospective obligation to the Notification dated

16.10.2023. We are also of the opinion that the approach adopted by the

High Court in applying principles of equity and estoppel against the

Appellant-College on the basis of its admission brochure is not

sustainable in law. To that extent, the judgment of the High Court is set

aside.

36.   For the reasons stated above, we partly allow Civil Appeals arising

out of SLP (C) No. 13237, 13690-13691, 16753, 14913-14914, 15617-


                                    25
15618 and 16677 of 2026, against the judgment and order of the High

Court in Writ Appeal MAT Nos. 268, 288, 284 of 2026, and direct that;

     (i) The fee fixation committees have a statutory foundation and have

     an important public purpose to subserve. The institutionalisation of

     these committees is necessary for realising the interests of aspiring

     students for professional higher education and also for establishing

     credible higher and professional educational institutions through

     private enterprise. High Courts will exercise due judicial review to

     ensure that these committees perform their duties with institutional

     efficiency, expertise, and integrity.

     (ii) The regulatory regime for fixation of fees, as contemplated in the

     decisions of this Court, AICTE Regulations, National Education

     Policy, 2020, coupled with principles of certainty, necessitates the

     relevant authorities to notify fee payable for the entire course before

     a student takes admission. There must be certainty about the fee

     liability; variation in the fee payable during the subsistence of the

     course is permissible only in exceptional instances such as

     unforeseen increase in the expenditure.

     (iii) The final directions of the High Court, as reproduced in

     paragraph 15 of this judgment with respect to applicability of the

     revised fees under Notification dated 16.10.2023 are affirmed. The

      Appellant-College will take necessary steps for complying with those

    all proceedings for contempt. If mere possibility of punishment were

    sufficient to place contempt within the fold of ‘criminal jurisdiction’, the

    carefully sustained distinction between the sui generis contempt

    jurisdiction and the ordinary criminal jurisdiction would lose its meaning,

    and the principle recognised in Chunilal Nanda (supra) would be

    rendered precarious. For the present discussion and subject to what we

    say hereafter, we would assume that Ram Kishan Fauji (supra) has

    legitimate, though limited, field of operation where the lis before the writ

    court is, in substance, criminal. But whether that principle can be

    pressed into service to oust an intra-court appeal in contempt

    proceedings, irrespective of the nature of the order and the jurisdiction

    actually exercised, is a question of some moment — more so, when

    several decisions of the High Court have proceeded on the premise that




                                       23
    contempt jurisdiction, wearing the garb of a criminal proceeding, bars a

    Special Appeal.

47. It is trite that criminal matter, criminal proceeding and criminal

    jurisdiction though inter-related are conceptually distinct. A criminal

    matter is the genus. It denotes the subject matter which has a criminal

    flavour, where penal consequence is involved. A crime committed, an

    offence alleged punishable under the IPC/BNS, an FIR or a complaint

    requiring investigation/inquiry – all are criminal matters at large. When

    that criminal matter is brought before a court of law or a competent

    authority in the form prescribed by law – be it an FIR, a complaint under

    Section 200, Cr. PC/Section 223, BNSS, a charge-sheet, a bail

    application, a revision, an appeal – the matter ripens and takes the form

    of a criminal proceeding. Every proceeding therefore is a matter, but

    every matter may not have yet become a proceeding. Criminal

    jurisdiction is the authority of the court to entertain, try and decide that

    criminal proceeding arising out of the criminal matter. It is the power to

    adjudicate. It is conferred by the statute, viz. the Cr. PC/BNSS or special

    law in terms of territory, subject matter and hierarchy. In short, a

    criminal matter gives rise to a criminal proceeding, which in turn can

    only be decided by a Court in exercise of its criminal jurisdiction. It is a

    progression: matter-> proceeding-> jurisdiction.

48. Having regard to our understanding of what ‘criminal jurisdiction’ is, the

    construction of ‘criminal jurisdiction’ in Ram Kishan Fauji (supra)

    cannot apply ex proprio vigore in contempt proceedings.


                                       24
49. Even otherwise, in the light of the foregoing discussion and for those to

    follow, we have our doubts as to whether Ram Kishan Fauji (supra)

    has laid down correct law on the interpretation of the Letters Patent

    governing the relevant high courts, the text of Article 226, and settled

    judicial principles regarding the exercise of power thereunder. The

    Constitution confers the power to issue prerogative writs under Article

    226 on the high courts for the enforcement of any of the Fundamental

    Rights or for any other purpose. It is a high prerogative, extraordinary

    original ‘Constitutional Writ Jurisdiction’. Writ remedy under Article 226,

    being a public law remedy, its invocation presupposes a public law

    element, i.e., infringement of a legally protected right and failure of

    public duty. Existence of the jurisdiction does not depend on whether

    the factual matrix originates in civil or criminal law. What is relevant is

    the nature of the grievance: whether a legally protected right has been

    infringed and also as to whether the right claimed is capable of being

    judicially enforced through a writ. The subject matter of a writ petition

    – whether having its roots in contract, service, taxation or criminal

    complaint – is not decisive of the nature of jurisdiction; what is decisive

    is the character of the lis and the nature of relief sought. Merely because

    the right asserted has its origin in a statute containing criminal elements

    cannot convert the special and exclusive constitutionally conferred ‘writ

    jurisdiction’ on the high courts into ordinary ‘criminal jurisdiction’ to

    defeat an intra-court appeal under the Letters Patent.




                                      25
50. Moving forward, the decision in Ram Kishan Fauji (supra), with

   respect, proceeds on the premise that Article 226 contains within it two

   jurisdictions – civil and criminal – and that the subject matter of the lis

   can determine the nature of the jurisdiction. Neither historical context

   nor the constitutional text nor the scheme of the Letters Patent nor

   settled judicial principle prior to such decision supports this division as

   well as the view that the writ court’s dealing with a criminal matter would

   amount to the exercise of ‘criminal jurisdiction’, thereby barring an intra-

   court appeal. The ratio that a writ arising from a criminal substratum is

   ‘criminal jurisdiction’ for clause 10 or clause 15 of the Letters Patent, as

   the case may be, is a judicial invention which the framers of the Letters

   Patent did never visualise, for, in 1862 there was no Article 226, and writ

   jurisdiction after the advent of the Constitution was itself not

   contemplated as civil or criminal. Article 226, in plain terms, confers a

   single, original, special, and extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction.

   Such jurisdiction is also neither civil nor criminal, but sui generis. It is

   also instructive that the very description or allocation of writ petitions

   before a High Court or this Court as ‘civil’ or ‘criminal’ does not, per se,

   furnish a principled basis for ascertaining the nature of the jurisdiction

   exercised under Article 226. Such classification is, at best, a matter of

   administrative convenience, designed to facilitate the allocation and

   listing of cases on the administrative side, and cannot be elevated into

   a substantive division of the constitutional jurisdiction conferred by

   Article 226. The mere fact that a writ petition is placed or described


                                      26
      under a ‘criminal’ category, for purposes of roster or administrative

      assignment, cannot convert the sui generis constitutional jurisdiction

      exercised therein into ‘criminal jurisdiction’. The jurisdiction remains, as

      conferred by Article 226; what may vary from case to case is the nature

      of the lis, the right asserted, and the relief sought. By importing the test

      of nature of subject matter, the decision in Ram Kishan Fauji (supra)

      converts exercise of jurisdiction in every writ petition involving any

      criminal element, be it a challenge to an FIR, an arrest, a chargesheet,

      an externment, etc., into ‘criminal jurisdiction’. The result is that an

      order refusing to quash an FIR, which determines criminal guilt of none

      and does not involve any punishment, is treated on a par with a

      conviction and sentence, thereby barring an intra-court appeal. Thus,

      what Ram Kishan Fauji (supra) does is to conflate the high prerogative

      writ jurisdiction with the ordinary criminal jurisdiction, and creates an

      asymmetry: an intra-court appeal arising out of a writ petition, say, in a

      land acquisition matter or in a taxation matter, would be permitted,

      which might involve infringement of Article 300A or Article 265 of the

      Constitution, respectively, which are non-Fundamental Rights, but when

      it comes to loss of liberty of a citizen under Article 21, he cannot. He

      would have, in such case, no other remedy but to approach this Court

      under Article 136 which, per the parent decision of this Court in Pritam

      Singh v. State33 interpreting Article 136, is discretionary, and the

      power thereunder should be exercised only in special circumstances. Not


33
     AIR 1950 SC 169

                                         27
       many people can afford to travel to Delhi to file a special leave petition.

       Long distance is not the only disabling factor; heavy expenses for

       boarding/lodging and for the proper presentation of a case and

       reasonable   representation   before   this   Court   are   also   involved,

       notwithstanding what science and technology have helped the system

       to achieve. The Constitution Bench in Anita Kushwaha v. Pushap

       Sudan34 has laid down the law that access to justice is a facet of Articles

       14 and 21. The wide and expansive writ jurisdiction which could be

       exercised by a Division Bench (an appeal being a continuation of the lis),

       to our mind, has been judicially restricted and curtailed in pursuance of

       an approach adopted in Ram Kishan Fauji (supra), which tends to

       violate Articles 14 and 39A; resultantly, it is access to justice which is

       rendered a casualty.

51. That apart, one cannot overlook that a right of appeal, being a creature

       of a statute, is not a matter of procedure but a substantive, vested and

       valuable right. However, where the language conferring a right of appeal

       is ambiguous or admits of two constructions, the Court must lean in

       favour of an expansive interpretation, not a restrictive one. It is the

       construction which enlarges and sustains the right, thereby, advancing

       the remedy that must be preferred to a narrow and constricted view

       which impairs or defeats such right. This particular aspect missed the

       notice of this Court while deciding Ram Kishan Fauji (supra).




 34
      (2016) 8 SCC 509

                                         28
52. We are conscious that the decision in Ram Kishan Fauji (supra) is a 3-

    Judge Bench decision, which would normally be binding on us.

    Nonetheless, for the reasons aforesaid, and more particularly the

    Constitution Bench decision in Anita Kushwaha (supra), we consider it

    proper to make a reference for consideration by an appropriate Bench,

    subject to such order as the Chief Justice of India may issue on the

    administrative side. The terms of reference are framed as follows:

       Does the decision in Ram Kishan Fauji v. State of Haryana, (2017)

       5 SCC 533 correctly interpret the Letters Patent governing the various

       high courts on maintainability of intra-court appeals in the light of the

       nature of jurisdiction conferred by Article 226 of the Constitution,

       adverted to above? Does the ratio not, effectively, negate proper

       access to justice at the intra-court appellate level, apart from creating

       a division in Article 226 not contemplated by the framers of the

       Letters Patent or the Constitution? Should the decision in Ram

       Kishan Fauji (supra) be revisited in view of the discussions in

       paragraphs 49 to 51 of this opinion?

53. Reverting to the case at hand, the directions given in the impugned order

    by the High Court have been noted above. The compliance affidavit

    containing the order of rejection passed in purported compliance with

    the order dated 17th March, 2026, has been rejected. Whether or not

    the Single Judge exceeded his jurisdiction in so rejecting is a matter that

    the appellant can well urge the Bench having determination to hear

    Special Appeals to examine.


                                       29
54. We, therefore, are not persuaded to entertain and examine the

    contentions raised by Mr. Nataraj on merits. The same are left open to

    be urged in a Special Appeal, which the appellant may present within a

    fortnight from the date of this order if so advised. If presented, the

    appeal may be decided on its own merits and in accordance with law by

    the appellate Bench.

55. The appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms. The reference

    made herein shall, however, remain pending for consideration by the

    appropriate Bench.

56. For a period of two months from this date, the contempt petition before

    the Single Judge shall remain stayed.

57. For the reasons recorded in paragraphs 49 to 51 and the questions

    framed in paragraph 52 hereinabove and in view of our consequent

    respectful disagreement with the enunciation of law in Ram Kishan

    Fauji (supra), this opinion may be placed by the Registry before the

    Chief Justice for appropriate orders on the administrative side.
